content.value: This sort of thing happens in lots of art forms, from film scores to standup sets. Depending on the medium, you might call it a theme, a callback, reincorporation. In music, the word motif describes a short, distinctive musical idea that recurs in a salient way.
Here are all of the motifs in Wicked.
These are all melodic motifs that are sung (excluding things happening in the orchestra), because those are the most obvious to perceive.
Musicals put motifs on display in a unique way.

Music is always telling a story, but here that is quite literal. This is especially true in musicals like Les Misérables or Hamilton where the entire story is told through song, with little to no dialogue. These musicals rely on motifs to create structure and meaning, to help tell the story.

Musicals like these are an excellent ground for observing the power and function of motifs – what exactly are they doing for the stories they are a part of? Let’s break that down, using examples from these sung-through musicals, but with patterns you’ll also spot across film, TV, and beyond.

value.dek: Visualizing how musicals use motifs to tell stories

content.value: Composers have been using repetition for forever. Think Beethoven’s 5th, where da-da-da-DUM repeats and reappears throughout the piece.

In the 19th century, German composers started formalizing the idea of attaching a motif to a person, place, or idea within a story (these are called leitmotifs). Think Peter and the Wolf, where different instruments and melodies represent different animals in the woods. Or the theme in “Up”, which captures the idea of Carl and Ellie’s shared life together.
So a motif doesn’t just exist, it represents something.

This creates a musical storytelling shortcut: when the audience hears a motif, that something is evoked. The audience can feel this information even if they can’t consciously perceive how it’s being delivered.

value.caption: In the first four minutes of Pixar’s Up, a melodic motif carries the emotional weight of the story, all without any dialogue.

content.value: This technique has been embraced in many mediums from opera to video game music to modern musical theater.
Let’s look at some examples of story and emotional information being conveyed through musical motifs.
Technique 1: Representing a character

One of the most straightforward uses of a motif is to represent a character in the story. These motifs can help cue the audience that a character is present, like Darth Vader or someone from the Fire Nation in Avatar the Last Airbender. A change in the motif’s instrumentation or tone can signal a change in that character.

notes.jvj-1: This motif is associated with Jean Valjean, the main character. It appears when he’s faced with a difficult decision, figuring out what to do.
notes.jvj-2: Jean Valjean gets an updated character motif right before the end of the first act, when the story fast forwards several years.
notes.cosette: This cute little melody is mostly associated with Cosette as a child, but we hear it again near the end of Act 1 when she’s all grown up.
notes.master-of-the-house: This represents The Thénardiers, the comic relief of the show who are always up to no good.

content.value: In Hamilton, there are often literal introductions of characters to a consistent melody or rhythm.
Technique 2: Representing an idea

More often, motifs are a marker for something more abstract – love, heartbreak, adventure – and not always owned by a specific character. Like this Star Wars theme that embodies the concept of The Force, calling in ideas around destiny, hope, the struggle between good and evil.

notes.look-down: One of the most important, enduring motifs of the show. Sung originally by a chain gang of prisoners, represents struggle and hard times.
notes.anguish: Sung in the darkest times of the battle, after someone important has died.
notes.god-on-high: Sounds like a hymn, Valjean praying / appealing to God. Represents mercy, divine protection, vulnerability of asking for help.
notes.drink-with-me: Sung by the students at the barricade, represents friendship and camaraderie in dark times.

content.value: Technique 3: Creating emotional layers

Why does that scene from “Up” make everyone cry? It establishes a simple melodic motif that comes to represent Carl & Ellie’s adventure together. But the real emotional weight comes from the fact that we hear it both in moments of joy and in moments of loss and heartbreak, each appearance carrying the previous memories with it. We feel the weight of the past layered onto the present moment, which makes it hit even harder.
The following motifs repeat, but with drastically different emotions across the show.

value.title: Les Misérables: Motifs with emotional changes

notes.friendship: Introduced at the very start when a bishop helps out Jean Valjean in a time of need, and brought back at the very end when Marius is grieving the loss of all his friends.
notes.lovely-ladies: Introduced early on when we meet the prostitutes, pimps, and sailors that surround Fantine. Comes back at the end when the women are reflecting on the battle and loss.
notes.rain: Sung first by Marius asking Eponine to do him a favor, in a moment where they connect. Comes back when Marius is holding Eponine as she is dying.
notes.little-people: This motif represents Gavroche, a courageous young kid who joins the rebellion. Introduced with a brave, joyful energy, and comes back when he is killed :(

notes.counting: This counting melody is both an introduction to the violent duel and a tune little Phillip sings and plays on the piano.
notes.i-imagine-death: Hamilton says “I imagine death so much it feels more like a memory” 3 times – going from contemplative to fearless to literally facing death.

content.value: Technique 4: Weaving everything together

Both Les Misérables and Hamilton have a song at the end of the first act where many of the motifs introduced so far all come together. The audience is reminded of everything we’ve learned and seen so far, and the most important threads of the story collide and are woven together.
There’s something else hidden within that “unlimited” theme from Wicked. It’s actually the same notes as “Somewhere Over The Rainbow”, a nod to the musical’s original source material.
Across generations, these pieces speak to each other, the threads connect. From the subtle to the more overt, connections like these shape how we feel and what sticks with us.
Most of us don’t consciously notice this force at work in the moment. Luckily, we don’t have to understand it to feel it.

hamilton.how-does-a: Sung by Aaron Burr, narrating and introducing a new part of the story.
hamilton.just-you-wait: Hamilton proving himself is a big theme throughout the musical.
hamilton.aaron-burr-sir: An exchange, usually between Burr and Hamilton.
hamilton.talk-less: A piece of advice Burr gives Hamilton (which he doesn’t take), that demonstrates the difference between them.
hamilton.i-imagine-death: Hamilton contemplating his legacy and mortality.
hamilton.raise-a-glass: Like 'Drink With Me' in Les Mis, this theme captures the camaraderie and idealism of young revolutionaries.
hamilton.look-around: This motif repeats lyrically in 'Non-Stop' and melodically in 'Schuyler Defeated'.
hamilton.angelica: Each Schyuler sister gets their own name motif.
hamilton.eliza: Each Schyuler sister gets their own name motif.
hamilton.schuyler-sisters: This one comes back very subtly in Act 2.
hamilton.youll-be-back: These 3 songs, sung by King George, are basically identical and musically distinct from the rest of the show.
hamilton.flashback: 'Satisfied' is a flashback of 'Helpless', and this motif helps place us in time as we experience the same events from a different angle.
hamilton.my-sister: Angelica demonstrating her fierce sisterly protection of Eliza.
hamilton.satisfied: This motif was borrowed from a letter from Angelica to Hamilton, where she writes: 'You are happy my dear friend to find consolation in “words and thoughts.” I cannot be so easily satisfied.'
hamilton.doesnt-discriminate: Burr contemplating two forces that are beyond his control, love and death.
hamilton.wait-for-it: Burr's main motif, representing his cautious, measured approach to life.
hamilton.counting: This count is usually used in the context of a duel, but also in 'Take a Break' for Phillip's piano lesson (some sad foreshadowing).
hamilton.duel-rules: These two songs are basically identical.
hamilton.aim-no-higher: The final rule, which recurs for each of the three duels in the show.
hamilton.that-would-be-enough: One of Eliza's main motifs, representing her love and devotion to Hamilton and their family.
hamilton.asking-me-to-lead: Washington's motif representing duty and leadership.
hamilton.history-has-its-eyes: One of the core themes of the show, this motif represents the weight of legacy.
hamilton.who-tells-your-story: This motif is the last thing we hear in the show, and sort of sums the whole thing up (in a very meta way).
hamilton.running-out-of-time: This motif is sung by other people about Hamilton and his relentless sense of urgency.
hamilton.phillip-rap: Phillip performs this rap for his parents as a 9-year old, and then again to himself when he's grown up, and feeling a little nervous.
hamilton.room-where-it-happens: Burr feels left out, even though his passiveness has put him there.
hamilton.on-your-side: Hamilton seems to be Washington’s favorite, and Burr, Jefferson, and Madison jealously sing about it.
hamilton.say-goodbye: Washington’s goodbye echoes in Hamilton’s final words.
hamilton.quiet-uptown: Hamilton calls back to the previous song about grieving the loss of his son while everyone around him in ‘The Election of 1800’ is focused on politics.

wicked.no-one-mourns: This motif is introduced in the first song, and comes back at the very end.
wicked.wicked: This ends the first and last song of the whole thing (in case you forgot which show you’re watching).
wicked.unlimited: The final time, the lyrics change from “unlimited” to “I’m limited.”
wicked.not-that-girl: First sung by Elphaba, then by Glinda, classic teen girl heartbreak.
wicked.no-good-deed: ‘No Good Deed’ is sort of the ‘Defying Gravity’ of Act 2 – we witness a big transformation in Elphaba.
wicked.for-good: Slight changes in pacing and harmony give the second appearance of this motif even more depth of emotion.

lesmis.24601: A confrontational motif between Jean Valjean and Javert.
lesmis.recitative: Recitative is a style of delivery used in opera where the singer adopts the rhythm and delivery of ordinary speech.
lesmis.valjean-rising: This rising melody is only sung by Valjean, when he’s faced with a difficult decision and figuring out what to do. It only sticks around for Act 1, and he gets an updated version in the second half of the show.
lesmis.friendship: This beautiful melody is introduced at the very start when a bishop helps out Jean Valjean in a time of need, and brought back at the very end when Marius is grieving the loss of all his friends.
lesmis.police: Often paired with Police 2, and usually shows up during a confrontation with the authorities.
lesmis.look-down: One of the most important, enduring motifs of the show. Sung originally by a chain gang of prisoners, represents struggle and hard times.
lesmis.reckoning: “Valjean’s Soliloquy” and “Javert’s Suicide” are identical melodically, and both represent moments of intense reckoning for these main characters. Fragments reappear in other songs in between.
lesmis.end-of-the-day: These songs depict Fantine’s desperate circumstances, and this theme is sung by some of the people antagonizing her.
lesmis.eod-authority: Sung by Valjean and later by Bamatabois who demands to buy Fantine's services as a prostitute, even after several refusals.
lesmis.tigers: First sung by Fantine, and carried on by others after she dies.
lesmis.dream: One of the most iconic motifs of the show, appearing in times of hope.
lesmis.lovely-ladies: Introduced early on when we meet the prostitutes, pimps, and sailors that surround Fantine. Comes back at the end when the women are reflecting on the battle and loss.
lesmis.honest-work: Sung by Javert and later by Enjoras, has a frustrated tone to it.
lesmis.turned-so-cold: Introduced when Fantine is dying, this motif comes back when Jean Valjean is dying and the ghost of Fantine welcomes him.
lesmis.who-am-i: The first time Valjean sings this, he’s debating whether to turn himself in and reveal his true identity. The final time he sings it, at the end of his life, he finally reveals the truth to his loved ones.
lesmis.im-jean-valjean: The first time Valjean sings this, he’s debating whether to turn himself in and reveal his true identity. The final time he sings it, at the end of his life, he finally reveals the truth to his loved ones.
lesmis.action: Sung by various people, this comes up in moments of action.
lesmis.condemned-damned: This descending melody is introduced by Jean Valjean in Act 1 and is sung by Eponine in Act 2.
lesmis.on-my-own: This is one of the most important motifs in the show – it’s introduced by Fantine as she’s dying, makes up the main melody of Eponine’s big number, and finally comes back when Valjean is dying and being guided by the voices of the fallen (including both Fantine and Eponine).
lesmis.on-my-own-b: The second section of the “On My Own” motif, which repeats in the same places.
lesmis.cosette: This cute little melody is mostly associated with Cosette as a child, but we hear it again near the end of Act 1 when she’s all grown up.
lesmis.cosette-b: The second section of Cosette’s motif.
lesmis.master-of-the-house: One of the Thenardier’s themes, the comic relief of the show.
lesmis.thenardier-waltz: The Thenardier’s other theme, sung when they’re manipulating or tricking someone.
lesmis.waltz-response: A response to the “Thenardier Waltz” motif.
lesmis.the-streets: This motif introduces Gavroche, and becomes a common one that Marius and Eponine sing to each other.
lesmis.panic: Associated with the Thenardiers, appears in stressful, panicked situations.
lesmis.forlorn: Both instances start with Marius and Eponine together, and end with a private confession from Eponine, who loves Marius but knows he doesn’t feel the same way.
lesmis.eponine: Sung only by Eponine or in scenes with Eponine, and has its final occurrence in the song where she dies.
lesmis.eponine-b: Sung only by Eponine or in scenes with Eponine, and has its final occurrence in the song where she dies.
lesmis.rain: Sung first by Marius asking Eponine to do him a favor, in a moment where they connect. Comes back when Marius is holding Eponine as she is dying.
lesmis.organizing: The students at the barricade coordinating.
lesmis.red-and-black: The rallying cry of the barricade.
lesmis.enjoras-2: Sung by Enjoras, rallying the students.
lesmis.the-people: A very important motif, representing the revolution of the people.
lesmis.the-people-b: The second section of the “The People” motif.
lesmis.valjean-rising-2: Jean Valjean gets an updated character motif right before the end of the first act, when the story fast forwards several years.
lesmis.heart-full-of-love: Representing Marius and Cosette’s love, this motif comes back at the end when they get married.
lesmis.heart-trio: In “A Heart Full of Love” this trio portion is sung by Marius, Cosette, and Eponine (looking on in longing). When it comes back in “Every Day”, Jean Valjean picks up the third part.
lesmis.letter: Introduced as Valjean reads a letter from Marius from Cosette, and comes back sung by Marius at the end.
lesmis.barricade: An off-stage voice of authority telling the students to give up (it’s obviously not funny, but “YOU HAVE NO FRIENDS” in “At The Barricade” always makes me laugh).
lesmis.watch: Sung as the students make a plan for the night watch.
lesmis.little-people: This motif represents Gavroche, a courageous young kid who joins the rebellion. Introduced with a brave, joyful energy, and comes back when he is killed.
lesmis.anguish: Sung in the darkest times of the battle, after someone important has died.
lesmis.god-on-high: This motif almost sounds like a hymn – it’s Valjean praying to God (first to protect Marius, later to declare he’s ready to die). Represents divine protection and the vulnerability of asking for help.
lesmis.drink-with-me: Sung by the students at the barricade, represents friendship and camaraderie in dark times.
